title: 2026 ASA Practice Guideline on Perioperative Pain Management Using Local and Regional Analgesia for Cardiothoracic Surgeries, Mastectomy, and Abdominal Surgeries
breakthrough: Procedure-specific recommendations for fascial plane blocks — TAP, erector spinae plane, serratus anterior and parasternal plane blocks — across cardiothoracic, mastectomy and abdominal surgery, replacing a one-technique-fits-all approach with guidance tied to the operation.
impact: From the ASA Task Force on Perioperative Pain Management. For ADULTS the recommendation is CONDITIONAL, and covers minimally invasive cardiothoracic surgery and open hernia repair. The STRONG recommendation is for CHILDREN after open cardiac or thoracic surgery. The Task Force notes its own evidence base was limited by low methodologic quality, inconsistent outcome measurement and small single-centre samples.
practical: Reduces 24-hour opioid consumption — up to roughly 60 mg oral morphine equivalents — and both rest and dynamic pain scores, which makes fascial plane blocks a reasonable default in opioid-sparing multimodal pathways. Treat the adult recommendation as conditional when weighing it against block time and expertise.
link: Anesthesiology - 2026 ASA guideline on regional analgesia

verify.note: The document is real and correctly cited. The original said the guideline elevated fascial plane blocks to 'Strong Recommendation' status for open surgeries in both adults and children. It is conditional for adults (and for minimally invasive cardiothoracic surgery plus open hernia repair, not open surgery generally); strong only for children after open cardiac or thoracic surgery. The guideline's own stated evidence limitations have been added.

title: Intervals for Oscillometric Arterial Pressure Monitoring during Noncardiac Surgery: The 2.5-Minute versus 5-Minute Randomized Clinical Trial
breakthrough: A negative trial. Cycling non-invasive oscillometric blood pressure every 2.5 minutes instead of every 5 did NOT reduce the time-weighted average of MAP below 65 mmHg. Both arms were nearly identical and both very low — almost certainly because 98% of the 264 patients were on norepinephrine infusions, which left little hypotension for faster measurement to catch.
impact: Does not displace the conventional 5-minute interval. The result is best read as showing that measurement frequency is not the binding constraint when hypotension is already being treated actively; it does not establish that 2.5-minute cycling is useless in a population managed without vasopressor infusions.
practical: No change to routine practice is warranted on this trial. Severe hypotension (MAP < 50 mmHg) was 5.3% versus 9.9%, P = 0.24 — a difference that looks appealing and is not statistically significant, in a single-centre trial of 264 patients. Treat it as a hypothesis, not a finding.
link: Anesthesiology - 2.5-minute vs 5-minute blood pressure monitoring trial

verify.status: corrected — original stated the opposite result
verify.note: The trial is real (NCT06314074) and it was NEGATIVE. The original said it proved shorter intervals reduce hypotensive depth and duration, and told readers to shorten NIBP cycling to 2.5 minutes during induction and high-risk phases — the opposite of what the trial found, and a practice change based on a null result. Rewritten to the actual finding, with the norepinephrine confound that explains it.

title: Videolaryngoscopy versus Direct Laryngoscopy for Double-Lumen Tube Intubation: The DOLVI Multicentre Randomized Trial
breakthrough: A multicentre randomized trial across four Spanish hospitals found videolaryngoscopy improved first-attempt success for double-lumen tube placement — 84.7% versus 76.9% — with better glottic visualisation, in patients requiring lung isolation for thoracic surgery.
impact: Glottic visualisation, oesophageal intubation and tube malposition were secondary outcomes and all favoured videolaryngoscopy. An accompanying BJA editorial asks whether this makes videolaryngoscopy the new standard for double-lumen placement; guidelines have not yet been revised, so this is the direction of travel rather than a change already made.
practical: Reduces procedural difficulty, loss of glottic view, oesophageal intubation and airway trauma with a tube that is large, stiff and awkward to place. A reasonable first choice where a videolaryngoscope is available.
link: British Journal of Anaesthesia - DOLVI multicentre trial

verify.note: Real and accurately summarised, including the first-attempt success figures. One softening: the original said the trial 'directly updates thoracic airway management guidelines'. It has not — that is the editorialist's question, not a guideline revision.

title: Management of Direct Oral Anticoagulants in Adult Patients Undergoing Cardiac Surgery: A Joint Consensus Statement by the SCA and STS
journal: Anesthesia & Analgesia / The Annals of Thoracic Surgery
breakthrough: One agreed approach to direct oral anticoagulants in adult cardiac surgery — cessation timing, laboratory monitoring, bridging, reversal and postoperative resumption — for patients going onto cardiopulmonary bypass.
impact: Published jointly by the Society of Cardiovascular Anesthesiologists and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons, appearing in both journals. Preoperative hold duration is keyed to renal function, with criteria distinguishing targeted reversal agents from prothrombin complex concentrates.
practical: Aims to reduce chest tube bleeding, transfusion and emergency re-operation while avoiding needless delay of urgent cases. Those are the consensus's stated objectives — a consensus statement does not itself measure them.
link: Anesthesia & Analgesia - SCA/STS joint DOAC consensus

verify.note: Real and correctly attributed. One softening: the original presented reduced bleeding, transfusion and re-operation as achieved outcomes. They are the consensus's goals; a consensus statement cannot demonstrate them.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Remimazolam Tosylate versus Propofol for Sedation of Postoperative Mechanically Ventilated Patients in Intensive Care Units: A Phase 3 Trial
breakthrough: A multicentre, randomized, single-blind, noninferiority phase 3 trial found remimazolam tosylate noninferior to propofol for SHORT-TERM sedation of postoperative mechanically ventilated ICU patients, and well tolerated. Mean terminal half-life 1.97 ± 1.62 h.
impact: Adds a flumazenil-reversible, organ-independent option alongside propofol for postoperative ventilated patients. No society guideline has been revised to incorporate it — this is a single phase 3 trial, not a change in standards.
practical: Companion trials report less hypotension with remimazolam, which is the practical draw in a patient who is already vasopressor-dependent. It also sidesteps propofol infusion syndrome and hypertriglyceridemia — but note the trial studied short-term sedation, so extended use is an extrapolation.
link: Anesthesiology - remimazolam vs propofol phase 3 trial

verify.note: Real (PMID 41855428, NCT06222294). Two fixes: the trial studied SHORT-TERM sedation, not 'prolonged postoperative mechanical ventilation' as the original title and practical implications both stated; and the original said it 'formally integrates remimazolam into PACU and surgical ICU guidelines', which has not happened.

title: Guidelines to the Practice of Anesthesia (Revised 2026 Edition)
breakthrough: The Canadian Anesthesiologists' Society's annual revision of its basic standards of anesthesia care — the 49th edition, and the 18th consecutive year published in the Canadian Journal of Anesthesia.
impact: CAS revises existing sections each year only where high-quality literature supports a change, and adds new sections as topics demand. It is the reference standard for anesthesia practice in Canada and is widely cited elsewhere.
practical: Worth reading annually rather than assuming the previous edition still applies, since the changes are targeted rather than announced. Consult the document itself for the current monitoring requirements and any environmental sustainability provisions.
link: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia - CAS Guidelines to the Practice of Anesthesia 2026

verify.status: corrected — two specific claims removed as unverified
verify.note: The document is real (PMID 41820767). Removed: 'a comprehensive overhaul', which contradicts CAS's own description of targeted annual revision; a new requirement for continuous micro-stream capnography in all sedation locations including NORA; and formal institutional plans to phase out desflurane. Those last two could not be confirmed from the abstract, and the proxy blocks the full text from this container. If they are in the document, they are worth stating — but they should be checked against it first, not asserted.

title: Electroencephalographic Monitoring in the Recovery Room for Identification of Patients at Risk for Postoperative Delirium
breakthrough: Automated frontal EEG in the immediate post-anaesthesia recovery period detected persistent slow-wave activity marking a 'vulnerable brain' phenotype, which was associated with increased risk of postoperative delirium before any clinical signs appeared.
impact: An association study, from Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin with Harvard and MIT collaborators. The authors propose that integrating recovery-room EEG into postoperative care may support risk stratification. No guideline has been changed.
practical: If it holds up, it would let PACU teams start delirium precautions — reorientation, structured analgesia, avoiding anticholinergics — before transfer to the ward, in the patients most likely to need them. Promising, not yet established as a screening test.
link: Anesthesiology - recovery-room EEG and delirium risk

verify.note: Real (PMID 41983562). Two softenings: 'accurately identifying patients at high risk' overstates a risk-association finding, and the original said the study 'refines perioperative brain health guidelines by recommending post-anesthesia EEG screening'. The authors propose it; no guideline recommends it.

title: Aspirin versus Clopidogrel for Chronic Maintenance Monotherapy after PCI: 10-Year Follow-up of the HOST-EXAM Trial
breakthrough: 5,438 patients in South Korea who had completed 6-18 months of DAPT after drug-eluting stent PCI without events, randomized to clopidogrel 75 mg or aspirin 100 mg and followed a median 10.5 years with 92.8% completeness. Clopidogrel was better for the primary composite — 25.4% versus 28.5%, HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.77-0.96), p = 0.0050 — and for both ischaemic and bleeding outcomes.
impact: Lower ischaemic AND bleeding events with clopidogrel, which is unusual and is what makes the trial notable. All-cause mortality did NOT differ — worth holding onto, because 'superior' here does not mean a survival benefit. Presented at ACC 2026 with simultaneous Lancet publication.
practical: Relevant preoperatively because more post-PCI patients presenting for elective noncardiac surgery will be on clopidogrel monotherapy rather than aspirin. Hold and restart timelines for chronic P2Y12 monotherapy follow from that, though the trial itself did not study the perioperative period.

verify.note: Real and accurately summarised. Added the trial's numbers and, importantly, that all-cause mortality did not differ — the original's 'maintains superior reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events' implies a mortality benefit that was not found. Also flagged that the perioperative implications are extrapolation.

title: Expert Consensus Statement on the Perioperative Management of Adult Patients Undergoing High-Risk Thyroidectomy
breakthrough: A consensus statement from the Society for Head and Neck Anesthesia covering intraoperative neural monitoring (IONM) protocols, vocal cord assessment, and emergency pathways for acute post-thyroidectomy haematoma.
impact: Standardises endotracheal tube positioning for recurrent laryngeal nerve monitoring — tube position determines whether IONM works at all — and sets out bedside wound decompression algorithms for airway compromise.
practical: Aims to reduce permanent vocal cord paralysis and speed response to post-thyroidectomy airway compromise on the ward. A post-thyroidectomy haematoma can obstruct the airway within minutes, and decompression cannot wait for return to theatre; a consensus statement sets the pathway but does not itself demonstrate a change in paralysis rates.
link: Anesthesia & Analgesia - high-risk thyroidectomy perioperative consensus

verify.note: Real (DOI 10.1213/ANE.0000000000008141, 10 June 2026). Two fixes: it is from the Society for Head and Neck Anesthesia, not 'multi-society'; and 'significantly reduces permanent vocal cord paralysis rates' is an intended benefit, not a measured outcome of a consensus statement.

title: Feasibility of a Multicomponent Protocol to Promote Dreaming during Surgical Anesthesia
breakthrough: A feasibility study of a five-part protocol: preinduction verbal priming about dreaming, propofol as the emergence anaesthetic, EEG-guided emergence, at least 10 minutes of minimised stimulation before emergence, and immediate postemergence interview. Of 452 patients interviewed, 69% reported dreaming — 93% among the 57 with full protocol adherence. 86% of dreams were positive and none very negative.
impact: A feasibility and safety signal, not a standards change. The protocol was safe with no awareness events and no difference in recovery times or analgesic and antiemetic use. Dreamers reported better sleep quality (9.16 ± 1.57 versus 7.65 ± 2.86).
practical: An unusually humane line of inquiry — what the patient experiences during and after anaesthesia, rather than only whether they were unconscious. Nothing here changes practice yet: the endpoint was dreaming, and larger trials would be needed to know whether it affects anything patients care about beyond sleep quality.
link: Anesthesiology - protocol to promote dreaming during anesthesia

verify.status: corrected — original credited it with outcomes it never measured
verify.note: The study is real but the original entry described it as an EEG-guided emergence bundle that markedly reduced emergence agitation and post-traumatic stress responses, and said processed EEG emergence tracking had entered post-anaesthesia recovery standards. It measured DREAMING. It did not measure agitation or PTSD, and no standard has changed. Rewritten to what the study actually did and found.
